fixes.explanation: Abimelech, the king of Gerar (Genesis 20:2), has nothing to do with this verse. Jacob doesn't name any king in his blessing to Joseph. He says Joseph's strong arms “…were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob…” (Genesis 49:24). That's God, friend, so a king was a fancy guess.

Potiphar, the captain of the guard who bought Joseph in Egypt (Genesis 39:1), isn't named here. Jacob doesn't mention any Egyptian official in this blessing. He says Joseph's strong arms “…were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob…” (Genesis 49:24). That's God.

Leaving isn't what Jacob brings up. His words are, “…what will happen to you in the days to come…” (Genesis 49:1). It's a talk about what's ahead for his sons. Pull up a chair, friend, not a suitcase.

Jacob says it right to him: “Reuben, you are my firstborn…” (Genesis 49:3). Firstborn means the oldest son, and Jacob calls him first. He also tells Reuben he is “…my might, and the beginning of my strength…” So Reuben is the one.

Jacob says, “May I never enter their council; may I never join their assembly.” (Genesis 49:6). He's talking about Simeon and Levi. Council and assembly, and he wants no part of either one. This is one of the heavy parts of the blessing.

Jacob says the opposite. His words about Simeon and Levi are, “May I never enter their council; may I never join their assembly.” (Genesis 49:6). He wants no part of either one. It's a heavy part of the blessing.

Right, he doesn't keep them together. Jacob says of Simeon and Levi, “I will disperse them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” (Genesis 49:7). Disperse and scatter both mean spreading out. It's a heavy part of the blessing.

No driving anybody out here. Jacob tells Judah, “…your brothers shall praise you.” (Genesis 49:8). He also says his father's sons “…shall bow down to you.” Praise and bowing, friend, not a push out the door.

Jacob says the reverse. His words are, “Like a lion he crouches and lies down; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him?” (Genesis 49:9). The way he asks it, the answer is nobody. If I were near that lion, I'd tiptoe so quietly even my mustache would hold its breath.

Jacob says the scepter stays with Judah “…until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his.” (Genesis 49:10). Allegiance means loyalty, friend. So the loyalty of the nations is his. Jacob's words reach way past his own sons.

Taking the scepter away is the opposite of what Jacob says. His words are, “The scepter will not depart from Judah…” (Genesis 49:10). Nobody takes it away in this verse. It stays with Judah “…until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his.”

Jacob says, “He washes his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.” (Genesis 49:11). Wine and the blood of grapes, friend. That picture is all about grapes. My laundry day has never looked like that.

Rainwater would be the plain guess, but it isn't what Jacob says. He says, “He washes his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.” (Genesis 49:11). The picture is all grapes and the vine. Nobody in this verse is reaching for a rain barrel.

Looking for more land isn't in this verse. Jacob says Issachar saw his land was pleasant, and then he “…bent his shoulder to the burden and submitted to labor as a servant.” (Genesis 49:15). The text gives him a burden to carry, not a search for more.

Driving flocks away isn't in this verse. Jacob says Issachar “…bent his shoulder to the burden and submitted to labor as a servant.” (Genesis 49:15). That comes right after Jacob calls him a strong donkey. Bending under a burden is what he does.

That rider is not staying in the saddle. Jacob says the viper “…bites the horse’s heels so that its rider tumbles backward.” (Genesis 49:17). Tumbles backward, friend. A snake in the path, and down goes the rider.
Right, the rider doesn't stay up there. Jacob says the viper “…bites the horse’s heels so that its rider tumbles backward.” (Genesis 49:17). Down he goes, backward. I would hate to be that rider.

Right, no dropping the bow here. Jacob says of Joseph, “Yet he steadied his bow, and his strong arms were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob…” (Genesis 49:24). The archers attacked him and aimed at him, and he steadied his bow. Steadying it is the opposite of dropping it.

Jacob says Joseph's strong arms “…were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob…” (Genesis 49:24). So the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob are right there in the picture of Joseph's strong arms. In the same sentence, Jacob also names “…the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel…”
Not an eagle. Jacob says, “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf…” (Genesis 49:27). In the morning he devours the prey, and in the evening he divides the plunder. A wolf it is, friend.

Right. The text says Jacob “…blessed each one with a suitable blessing.” (Genesis 49:28). Judah is pictured as a young lion, and Zebulun is told he will dwell by the seashore and become a harbor for ships. Different pictures for different sons.

Jacob says, “Bury me with my fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite.” (Genesis 49:29). Fathers is his word, friend. He says Abraham and Sarah are buried in that cave, and Isaac and Rebekah too (Genesis 49:31). So the fathers he means are already resting there.
Jacob isn't asking to be buried in Egypt. He says the cave is “…in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 49:30). Egypt isn't the land he names for his burial. Canaan is.
